declarations.name: SheepButtonComponent
declarations.summary: A styled button.
declarations.description:
A styled button.

Renders a native `<button>`, so keyboard, form submission and screen-reader
behaviour come for free. Content projects into three slots:

```html
<sheep-button tone="danger" variant="solid">
  <svg sheepButtonStart>...</svg>
  Delete project
</sheep-button>
```

`shape="square"` is the icon-only form: a 1:1 box at the control height,
which is the whole of what an icon button is. There is no separate
`sheep-icon-button`, and deliberately so — a second component would have to
re-expose these same variants, tones and sizes, and the two would drift.
An icon-only button carries no text, so it needs `ariaLabel` to have a name
at all; a dev-mode check below says so out loud when it is missing.

Deliberately NOT themeable per instance. Every colour and metric comes from
the `--sheep-*` theme layer, so two buttons in one app cannot drift apart.
To change how buttons look, change the theme.

declarations.name: SheepInputComponent
declarations.summary: A single-line text input.
declarations.description: A single-line text input. Renders a real ``, so typing, selection, autofill, IME composition and the password manager are the platform's rather than a reimplementation. The component owns the label, the hint, the error line and the box around them, and wires the `id` / `aria-describedby` / `aria-invalid` between them: ```html Display name Shown on your profile. ``` It implements signal forms' `FormValueControl`, so `[formField]` binds it end to end — value, errors, disabled, readonly, touched, and the `required` / `minLength` / `maxLength` / `pattern` constraints, which reach the native input as real attributes: ```html Email ``` Everything past a value and a label is a directive on the host element — `sheepPassword`, `sheepEmail`, `sheepNumber`, `sheepCounter`, `sheepValidate` — so a plain field carries none of their weight. See `SheepInputFeature`. The field is a rule, not a box: one hairline under the value, with empty space doing the framing. Its label floats — resting inside the box in place of a placeholder, lifting to the row above on focus or once there is a value, without the box moving. Deliberately NOT themeable per instance. Every colour and metric comes from the `--sheep-*` theme layer, and the two appearance inputs pick between spec'd looks rather than opening one up.

declarations.name: SheepInputPasswordDirective
declarations.summary: Turns the field into a password field with a reveal toggle.
declarations.description: Turns the field into a password field with a reveal toggle. ```html Password ``` It sets the type itself, so there is no `type="password"` to keep in sync beside it — masking and the affordance to unmask are one decision, and this directive is where it is made. While revealed the input really is `type ="text"`: nothing else unmasks a password field, and a fake mask would defeat selection, autofill and the password manager. The toggle is a real focusable button so a keyboard user can reach it, but it takes no focus on a mouse click, so the caret stays where it was mid-word. Its accessible name comes from `SHEEP_INPUT_MESSAGES`. Leave `autocomplete` to the call site: only it knows whether this is the password being entered (`current-password`) or chosen (`new-password`), and getting that wrong is what makes a manager fill the wrong box.

declarations.name: SheepInputEmailDirective
declarations.summary: Turns the field into an email field: the type, the keyboard, and the check.
declarations.description: Turns the field into an email field: the type, the keyboard, and the check. ```html Work email ``` Beyond `type="email"` it turns off the four things a phone keyboard does to an address — capitalise it, autocorrect it, spellcheck it, and hide the `@` behind a shift — which is most of why hand-rolled email fields are painful on mobile. An empty value is not an error here; that is `required`'s question, and answering it twice would show two messages for one blank field. **Who owns validity.** This raises an error the *field* renders. A signal form cannot see it, so a form-bound field would show the message while the form still considered itself valid. On a form-bound field, put `email()` in the schema instead and drop this directive's validation half — reach for it on a field with no form behind it, or one in a template-driven form. The same applies to `sheepValidate`.

declarations.name: SheepInputNumberDirective
declarations.summary: Turns the field into a number field: the keyboard, the filter, the arrows and the check.
declarations.description: Turns the field into a number field: the keyboard, the filter, the arrows and the check. ```html Age Price $ ``` The `` stays `type="text"`. Native `type="number"` is the thing this is built to avoid: a mouse wheel over a focused field changes the value while the user means to scroll the page, `e` and `+` are accepted, and input the browser cannot parse reads back as an empty string, so a typo looks like a blank field to the form. What it does instead: - **Keyboard.** A number pad on a phone — `numeric` for whole numbers, `decimal` when `step` allows a fraction. When `min` allows a negative, the full keyboard is kept, because the phone number pads have no minus key; set `min="0"` to get the pad. - **Filter.** A keystroke or paste that could not become a number is refused: letters, a second point, a minus that is not first or that `min` rules out, a point when `step` is whole. - **Arrows.** Arrow Up and Down add and take away `step` (1 by default), held within `min` and `max`. - **Check.** `number`, `min`, `max` and `step` errors, shown once the field is touched, worded by the message table. An empty value is not an error; that is `required`'s question. The value stays a string, the same as every other field, so `"007"` and `"1.50"` survive as typed. Convert at the edge — `Number(value)` where the value is used — and keep in mind that `""` is "nothing entered", not zero. The point is always `.`. Fields that must accept a locale's decimal comma are not covered. **Who owns validity.** As with `sheepEmail`: the errors raised here are the field's, and a signal form cannot see them. On a form-bound field, put `min()` / `max()` in the schema too.

declarations.name: SheepInputValidateDirective
declarations.summary: A rule of the caller's own, run over the value on every keystroke.
declarations.description:
A rule of the caller's own, run over the value on every keystroke.

Return `null` when the value is fine, a string to say what is wrong, or
`SheepFieldError`s when the message belongs in the message table rather than
at the call site:

```ts
protected readonly notReserved = (value: string) =>
  RESERVED.has(value.toLowerCase()) ? 'That name is taken.' : null;
```
```html
<sheep-input [sheepValidate]="notReserved">
```

declarations.name: SheepDialogComponent
declarations.summary: A modal popup.
declarations.description:
A modal popup.

The dialog owns being open, being modal and being dismissed. It owns nothing
about what is inside it: the three parts are slots, and the caller fills
them with their own content and their own buttons.

```html
<sheep-dialog [(open)]="confirming">
  <sheep-dialog-header>Delete project</sheep-dialog-header>
  <sheep-dialog-body>This cannot be undone.</sheep-dialog-body>
  <sheep-dialog-footer>
    <sheep-button (click)="confirming.set(false)">Cancel</sheep-button>
    <sheep-button tone="danger" variant="solid" (click)="remove()">
      Delete
    </sheep-button>
  </sheep-dialog-footer>
</sheep-dialog>
```

The parts are ordered by the component, not by the markup: the header is
always the first row and the footer always the last, so a dialog cannot be
assembled upside down. The body is the only part that scrolls — the panel
stops growing at the viewport and the header and footer stay put.

Underneath is a native `<dialog>` opened with `showModal()`, so the focus
trap, the backdrop, the top-layer stacking and Escape are the platform's,
not a reimplementation of them. It follows that an ancestor's `overflow` or
`transform` cannot clip the panel, and that no z-index needs choosing.

`open` is the state, and it is two-way: nothing else opens or closes the
dialog behind the caller's back. A dismissal — Escape, a click on the
backdrop, the header's close button — writes `false` back and says why
through `closed`.

A modal needs an accessible name. A `sheep-dialog-header` supplies one; a
dialog without a header wants `ariaLabel`.

Deliberately NOT themeable per instance. Every colour and metric comes from
the `--sheep-*` theme layer, so two dialogs in one app cannot drift apart.

declarations.name: SheepTableComponent
declarations.summary: A table.
declarations.description:
A table.

Composed, not configured. The table owns the data and everything done to it —
filtering, sorting, paging — and owns none of what is drawn: each column is
declared once, at the call site, as a name and two templates.

```html
<sheep-table [data]="employees()">
  <ng-container sheepColumnDef="name" sortable filterable>
    <sheep-header-cell *sheepHeaderCellDef>Name</sheep-header-cell>
    <sheep-cell *sheepCellDef="let row">{{ row.name }}</sheep-cell>
  </ng-container>

  <ng-container sheepColumnDef="salary" sortable align="end" width="120px">
    <sheep-header-cell *sheepHeaderCellDef>Salary</sheep-header-cell>
    <sheep-cell *sheepCellDef="let row">{{ row.salary | currency }}</sheep-cell>
  </ng-container>
</sheep-table>
```

That is the whole table: no row template to keep in sync with a column list,
no `displayedColumns` array unless the columns are meant to change, and no
data source object between the array and the screen. Built on CDK's
`cdkTable`, so the row and cell recycling, the sticky positioning and the
virtual-scroll wiring are theirs rather than a second implementation.

### Paging, and when it stops

A paginator sits under the table by default. Past `virtualThreshold` rows it
goes away and the table virtualises instead — one continuous scroll with
about a screenful in the DOM. Paging through four hundred pages is not
navigation, and rendering four hundred pages at once is not free; at that
size scrolling is the honest control.

Either way the DOM holds a window, never the whole set: while paging, the
rows of one page; while virtualised, the rows on screen. The switch is
measured against the *filtered* rows, so narrowing a large table hands the
paginator back.

### Sorting and filtering

A column declares `sortable` or `filterable` and its header grows the
control. Both default to reading the property the column is named after, and
both are overridable per column — `sortAccessor` and `filterAccessor` for the
value, `sortComparator` and `filterPredicate` for the whole decision. See
`sheepColumnDef`.

A filter opens in a panel rather than sitting under the header: a row of
boxes doubles the height of every table that has one filterable column, and
charges that on every screen whether or not anything is being filtered.

`sort` and `filters` are two-way: bind them to open on a sorted column, to
persist a view in the URL, or to drive the table from elsewhere on the page.

### Width

Columns share the frame, flexing against each other, and a column can name a
`width` to opt out or a `grow` to take more of what is left. None of them
shrinks past a floor set by the density — below that the frame scrolls
sideways instead, which is what a `sticky` column is for.

Deliberately NOT themeable per instance. Every colour and metric comes from
the `--sheep-*` theme layer; `size` picks between spec'd densities rather
than opening one up.

`cdk-virtual-scroll-viewport` is not clipped at the edge of the viewport.

current state rather than a copy taken when it opened: when an anchor's text
changes under it — a recycled row, a value that ticks — the words on screen
change with it, and the box is measured and placed again around them.

declarations.description:
Owns the one tooltip surface, and which anchor currently has it.

a service rather than a component each directive creates is the count. A
virtualised list has a `sheepTooltip` on every rendered row and a thousand
more waiting to be recycled into, and only ever one tooltip is on screen.

think about them: a row scrolls away and its directive is destroyed after
the pointer has already opened the next row's tooltip, and its `hide` is a
no-op rather than a tooltip that vanishes from under the pointer.

declarations.name: SheepTooltipDirective
declarations.summary: A short label explaining the element it is put on.
declarations.description:
A short label explaining the element it is put on.

```html
<sheep-button [sheepTooltip]="'Archive ' + folder.name">
  Archive
</sheep-button>
```

Put it on anything — a button, an icon, a truncated cell. The directive adds
no element and no wrapper, so nothing about the layout changes by describing
something. Opens on hover and on focus, closes on leave, blur and Escape.

### It is a description, not a name

The tooltip becomes the anchor's `aria-describedby`, which is the right role
for a note *about* a control that already says what it is. An icon-only
button has no name for a tooltip to elaborate on, so give it an `aria-label`
as well — a tooltip is not a substitute, because it is not there when the
pointer is not.

### The text is live

`sheepTooltip` is read as a signal, not copied when the tooltip opens. Bind
a value that changes and the open tooltip changes with it, re-measuring
around the new words. Setting it to an empty string closes it: there is no
separate "and now hide it" to keep in step with the text.

### Virtual scroll

Works on a row of a `cdk-virtual-scroll-viewport` with nothing extra asked
of the caller. The surface is a native `popover` in the top layer, so the
viewport's own `overflow` cannot clip it, and it tracks its anchor's box
while anything scrolls rather than staying at the coordinates it opened at.

A viewport does not destroy the row that scrolls away — it recycles the view
and pours the next row's data through it — so the anchor under a resting
pointer stays put and changes what it holds. Because the text is live, the
tooltip changes with it and goes on describing whatever is actually under
the pointer. The destroy path covers the other case, where the view really
is torn down; either way nothing is left pointing at a row that has gone.

Deliberately NOT themeable per instance. Every colour and metric comes from
the `--sheep-*` theme layer.

The label is an input, not a projected slot, and that is deliberate: what the badge *is* depends on whether it has one. With a label it is a pill; with an icon and no label it is a circle sized to the icon; with both it is a pill with a leading icon. A badge is the exception, on purpose and within a boundary: badges routinely paint data the design system has never seen. A label colour a user picked, a per-tenant brand, a category colour that came out of a database. There is no variant to add to the spec for a colour that does not exist until runtime. So three custom properties are public API: | Property | What it sets | | --- | --- | | `--sheep-badge-color` | The hue. Both weights are derived from it. | | `--sheep-badge-text` | The label colour, overriding what the hue implies. | | `--sheep-badge-icon` | The icon colour. Defaults to the label colour. | The `color`, `textColor` and `iconColor` inputs are the same three knobs from TypeScript — they write those properties onto the host and nothing else. Set them from a stylesheet instead when the colour belongs to a context rather than to one badge: ```css .tenant-acme sheep-badge { --sheep-badge-color: #0f6fff; } ``` Note what is *not* here: no padding, no radius, no font, no border hooks. declarations.summary: A modal panel anchored to the left or right edge of the viewport.
declarations.description:
A modal panel anchored to the left or right edge of the viewport.

The sheet owns being open, being modal and being dismissed. It owns nothing
about what is inside it: the three parts are slots, and the caller fills
them with their own content and their own buttons.

```html
<sheep-side-sheet [(open)]="filtering" side="right">
  <sheep-side-sheet-header>Filters</sheep-side-sheet-header>
  <sheep-side-sheet-body>
    <sheep-chip-set>...</sheep-chip-set>
  </sheep-side-sheet-body>
  <sheep-side-sheet-footer align="between">
    <sheep-button variant="ghost" (click)="reset()">Reset</sheep-button>
    <sheep-button variant="solid" (click)="apply()">Apply</sheep-button>
  </sheep-side-sheet-footer>
</sheep-side-sheet>
```

It is `sheep-dialog` moved to an edge, and deliberately so: same parts, same
state, same dismissal, same three close reasons. What differs is the
geometry and what that geometry is for. A dialog interrupts to ask one
question and wants an answer before the page continues; a sheet comes in
beside the page to hold a secondary surface — filters, a detail record, a
form — that the user works in and then puts away. Reach for a dialog when
the page must stop, and for a sheet when it merely steps aside.

The parts are ordered by the component, not by the markup: the header is
always the first row and the footer always the last, so a sheet cannot be
assembled upside down. The body is the only part that scrolls — the panel is
always the full height of the viewport, and the header and footer stay put.

Underneath is a native `<dialog>` opened with `showModal()`, so the focus
trap, the backdrop, the top-layer stacking and Escape are the platform's,
not a reimplementation of them. It follows that an ancestor overflow or
transform cannot clip the panel, and that no z-index needs choosing.

`open` is the state, and it is two-way: nothing else opens or closes the
sheet behind the caller's back. A dismissal — Escape, a click on the
backdrop, the header's close button — writes `false` back and says why
through `closed`.

A modal needs an accessible name. A `sheep-side-sheet-header` supplies one;
a sheet without a header wants `ariaLabel`.

Deliberately NOT themeable per instance. Every colour and metric comes from
the `--sheep-*` theme layer, so two sheets in one app cannot drift apart.

declarations.name: SheepTreeComponent
declarations.summary: A collapsible hierarchy.
declarations.description:
A collapsible hierarchy.

```html
<sheep-tree
  [nodes]="folders"
  [(expanded)]="open"
  [(selected)]="current"
/>
```

## Why this does not nest

The obvious way to build a tree is a component that renders itself once per
child. It is also the slow way, and the cost lands exactly where a tree is
supposed to be good: depth. Every level adds a component instance, an
embedded view and a change-detection node per node, stacked into a view
hierarchy as deep as the data, so work grows with depth as well as with
count and a change near the root walks everything under it.

This tree does not nest. `rows` flattens the visible nodes into one array in
a single `computed()`, and the template is one flat `@for` over it. Depth
becomes `--_tree-level`, which the stylesheet turns into padding. A node
twelve levels down is one row, the same one DOM row as a node at the top,
and the view hierarchy is one level deep no matter what the data does.

Three things follow from that, and they are the whole performance story:

- **Collapsed subtrees cost nothing.** The flatten walks into a node only
  when it is expanded, so the work is proportional to what is on screen, not
  to what is in the data. A collapsed million-node branch is one row.
- **Expanding is a splice, not a subtree build.** The `computed()` reruns,
  `@for` tracks by node id, and Angular adds exactly the new rows. Nothing
  above or beside them is touched.
- **It virtualizes.** Every row is one line at a fixed height whatever its
  depth, so a flat run can be dropped in a `cdk-virtual-scroll-viewport`
  with `SHEEP_TREE_ROW_HEIGHT` as `itemSize` — which a nested tree cannot
  do at all, since its rows are not siblings.

## State

The caller owns both pieces of state and both are two-way. `expanded` is a
set of node ids, so expansion survives the data being replaced and a caller
can open a path by writing the ids into it. `selected` is a single id, or
null. Nothing is stored on the nodes themselves, so the caller data stays
the caller data.

Keyboard is the standard tree: up and down move, right expands or steps in,
left collapses or steps out, Home and End jump, Enter and Space select. One
row is in the tab order at a time.

Deliberately NOT themeable per instance. Every colour and metric comes from
the `--sheep-*` theme layer, so two trees in one app cannot drift apart.
